title: Raw Sockets
intro: You already await async I/O at work. What you haven't done is see what's underneath it. Eight sessions, and by the last one you're assembling pieces you've already built — not writing an echo server from a blank page.

days.title: A socket is a file descriptor
days.teaser: What socket() actually allocates, and why it hands you an int.
days.theoryMarkdown:
### What a socket actually is (not just "it's an int")

The `int` you get back from `socket()` is not the socket. It's a **handle** — an
index into your process's file descriptor table, which the kernel uses to look up the
real thing. The real thing is a kernel-side data structure that bundles together:

- the local address/port it's bound to (once you `bind()`)
- the remote address/port it's connected to (once you `connect()`/`accept()`)
- protocol state — for TCP specifically, this is a whole state machine
  (`LISTEN`, `SYN_SENT`, `ESTABLISHED`, `CLOSE_WAIT`, ...) that the kernel drives
  as packets arrive, entirely outside your process
- send and receive buffers — the kernel is buffering bytes on your behalf before
  your process ever calls `recv()`, which is exactly why short reads happen (more on
  that on Day 5/6)

So "a socket" is really closer to "a live object the kernel maintains on your
process's behalf," and your `int` is a ticket you hand back to the kernel every time
you want to do something with it (`send(fd, ...)`, `recv(fd, ...)`, `close(fd)`). This
is the same relationship a regular file fd has to the actual open-file state — sockets
were deliberately designed to slot into the exact same fd table as files, pipes, and
terminals, so the same `read`/`write`/`close`/`select` machinery works on all of them
almost interchangeably. That unification is arguably the single best design decision
in the whole API.

### Is this still how it actually works today?

Yes, genuinely — this isn't legacy cruft you're learning for historical interest.
Every mainstream networking stack — Boost.Asio, Python's `socket` module, Node's
`net`, Go's `net` package, the JVM's NIO — is, at the bottom, opening one of these
exact same fds with this exact same syscall. Asio's `async_read` eventually calls
`recv()` on a fd it got from `socket()`; it just also manages an event loop
(`epoll`/`io_uring`/IOCP depending on OS) so it doesn't have to block on it. You're not
learning a museum piece, you're learning the floor everything else stands on. Even
Windows agrees here — Winsock, Microsoft's socket API, is a near-clone of this same
BSD interface from the 1990s, because by then everyone had already agreed this was the
right shape.

What *has* changed over 40+ years is how you find out a socket is ready to be
read/written without blocking a whole thread on it — `select()` → `poll()` → `epoll()`
→ `io_uring` is basically the entire history of Linux I/O scalability in one line. But
notice: all of those are about *notification*, not about replacing the socket
abstraction itself. The fd and the `socket()`/`bind()`/`connect()` shape have been
stable since 1983.

### The call itself

```cpp
int fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
```

Three arguments, three questions:

- **`AF_INET`** — *address family*. What kind of address will this socket use?
  `AF_INET` = IPv4. (`AF_INET6` for IPv6, `AF_UNIX` for local-machine-only sockets —
  same syscall, different address shape entirely.)
- **`SOCK_STREAM`** — *socket type*. What delivery guarantee do you want?
  `SOCK_STREAM` = TCP: reliable, ordered, connection-based byte stream. (`SOCK_DGRAM`
  = UDP: fire-and-forget packets, no connection.)
- **`0`** — *protocol*. Almost always `0`, meaning "pick the default protocol for that
  family+type combo" (TCP for `AF_INET`+`SOCK_STREAM`). You'd only set this
  explicitly in exotic cases (e.g. raw ICMP sockets).

On success: a small positive int, the fd. On failure: `-1`, with `errno` set — the
universal POSIX pattern of "sentinel return value, check `errno` for why," which is
why `strerror(errno)` shows up constantly in this milestone. `errno` itself predates
sockets by over a decade — it's a 7th-Edition-Unix-era (1979) mechanism, bolted onto
every syscall API that came after it, sockets included.

### What's still missing at this point

`socket()` only allocates the resource — it doesn't bind an address, doesn't listen,
doesn't connect. `bind()`, `listen()`, `accept()`/`connect()` are separate calls that
come on later days and give this fd an actual role. Allocate, then configure, then
use — that three-step shape repeats throughout this API.

### One more bit of trivia, since you asked for it

The name "socket" itself is a deliberate metaphor from the original design at UC
Berkeley (funded by DARPA, released as part of 4.2BSD in 1983): an endpoint you plug a
connection into, the same way you'd plug something into a wall socket or a phone jack.
The API predates HTTP by about eight years and predates "the web" as a concept
entirely — TCP/IP networking on Unix existed, and needed a programming interface,
before there was anything resembling a browser to use it.

quiz.prompt: What does it mean if socket() returns -1 versus returning 3?

options.text: -1 specifically means the kernel is out of memory
options.why: -1 is generic on purpose. Collapsing every failure into one return value is exactly why errno exists as a second channel — one bit of "it broke" plus a separate "here's which way".

options.text: -1 is failure and errno says why; 3 is a valid fd — the lowest free slot in the table
options.why: Both halves matter. -1 is a sentinel meaning "look at errno" — the specific reason (EMFILE, ENFILE, EACCES, EAFNOSUPPORT) lives there, not in the return value. And 3 isn't arbitrary: POSIX guarantees the lowest available fd, and 0/1/2 are already stdin/stdout/stderr, so a first socket in a normal process is almost always 3.

options.text: -1 is success and 3 is an error code, like functions that return 0 on success
options.why: Inverted, and it's a real confusion because POSIX has both conventions. Calls that *return a resource* (socket, open, accept) return the resource and use -1 for failure. Calls that only report status (pthread_create, most of the pthreads API) return 0 on success and an error number directly.

options.text: -1 means no client has connected yet; 3 means one has
options.why: socket() hasn't touched the network at all — no address, no port, no packet. It cannot possibly know anything about clients. That's accept()'s job, four days from now.

quiz.prompt: Why is the fd from socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0) not yet listening or connected to anything — what's missing?

options.text: It has no address. socket() allocates the object; bind()/connect() give it a role
options.why: Allocate, then configure, then use — the three-step shape that repeats all over this API. Right now the kernel has a TCP socket in state CLOSED with no local address, no remote address, and nothing in its buffers.

options.text: The protocol argument is 0, which leaves it unusable until you pass IPPROTO_TCP
options.why: 0 means "the default protocol for this family and type" — which for AF_INET + SOCK_STREAM is exactly IPPROTO_TCP. Passing it explicitly changes nothing. You'd only set it for exotic cases like raw ICMP sockets.

options.text: It isn't backed by a file yet, and every fd ultimately refers to a file on disk
options.why: An fd is a handle to any kernel object that implements the file interface — sockets, pipes, terminals, epoll instances, timers. No disk is involved. That unification is the best design decision in the whole API: read/write/close work on all of them.

options.text: Nothing's missing — the kernel already picked an ephemeral port for it
options.why: No port is reserved until bind(), or until connect() does an implicit bind on your behalf. Until then the socket owns no part of the port space, which is why two processes can both call socket() and neither conflicts.

quiz.prompt: If you called socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM, 0) instead, what changes about the guarantees?

options.text: Nothing changes until you call sendto() — the type only picks which functions are legal
options.why: The type selects the transport protocol right there in socket(). The kernel builds a UDP socket, not a TCP one, from that call onward — different state machine, different everything.

options.text: You still get an ordered byte stream, just without connection setup
options.why: Ordered byte stream is the one thing UDP is not. Datagrams preserve message boundaries precisely because there's no stream to order them into.

options.text: You lose reliability and ordering, but gain message boundaries: one send is one recv
options.why: UDP datagrams can be dropped, duplicated, or arrive out of order, and nothing retransmits them. In exchange each datagram stays a discrete unit — the exact opposite of the byte-stream problem that will bite you on Day 6.

options.text: It's still reliable, just faster, because UDP skips the three-way handshake
options.why: This conflates latency with delivery guarantee. Skipping the handshake is real, but there are also no acknowledgements and no retransmission, so the network is entirely free to drop your datagram and never tell you.

quiz.prompt: A program calls socket() ten thousand times in a loop and never calls close(). What actually runs out, and how does it show up?

options.text: The fd table — you hit RLIMIT_NOFILE and socket() starts returning -1 with errno EMFILE
options.why: Every fd is a slot in a per-process table with a hard ceiling (`ulimit -n`, often 1024 or 8192). The failure is quiet and late: nine thousand calls succeed, then everything fails at once — which is why "check the return value of every syscall" stops sounding paranoid. EMFILE is per-process; ENFILE is the system-wide table, and seeing that one means you've taken the whole box down, not just yourself.

options.text: Nothing — a socket with no address bound holds no resources until you bind() it
options.why: The kernel allocated a real structure the moment socket() returned: buffers, protocol state, a table slot. Unbound just means the address fields are empty. This is the fd-leak bug in a nutshell — it looks free because nothing visible happened.

options.text: Nothing — the kernel reclaims sockets that have no address once memory gets tight
options.why: There's no garbage collector here. The fd is a reference the kernel assumes you still want; it's released when you close it or when the process exits. Process exit is the only cleanup you get for free, which is exactly why a long-lived server leaking fds is so much worse than a short script doing it.

options.text: The ephemeral port range — 65535 ports means you run out of ports long before fds
options.why: Plausible arithmetic, wrong stage. No port is reserved until bind() or connect(); these sockets never touched the port space. Port exhaustion is real, but it's a client-side problem you hit by opening lots of *connections* — and it's why TIME_WAIT shows up in your life later.

quiz.prompt: When Asio hands you `co_await socket.async_read_some(...)`, what has replaced the raw recv() call underneath?

options.text: Asio uses a userspace TCP stack to skip the syscall, which is where the speedup comes from
options.why: Kernel-bypass stacks exist (DPDK, and the reason people say "userspace TCP"), but they're a specialist tool for line-rate packet processing, and Asio isn't one. Ordinary Asio is a thin, portable wrapper over the kernel's sockets.

options.text: io_uring replaced the socket API — modern async I/O submits operations directly, with no fd
options.why: io_uring changed how you *submit and complete* work, not what you're operating on: its ops take the same fd from the same socket() call. Forty years in, the notification mechanism has been rewritten four times and the socket abstraction hasn't moved.

options.text: It's the same recv(), but Asio runs it on a worker thread so the blocking wait is off your coroutine
options.why: That's the thread-pool model — real, and what some libraries genuinely do, but it's the design Asio exists to avoid. A thread parked in a blocking recv() costs you a stack and a context switch per connection; readiness notification costs you one epoll entry. This distinction is precisely why C10k was a named problem.

options.text: Nothing — it's still recv() on an fd from socket(); what Asio adds is knowing when to call it
options.why: This is the whole point of Day 1. Asio owns an event loop (epoll on Linux, kqueue on BSD, IOCP on Windows) that watches the fd and resumes your coroutine once the kernel says data has arrived — then does the ordinary recv(). The abstraction you already use at work is a scheduler bolted on top of the exact three calls in this milestone.

task.markdown:
Write a program that:

1. Calls `socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0)`
2. Checks the return value — on failure, print `strerror(errno)` and exit with a
   non-zero status
3. On success, prints the fd
4. Calls `close(fd)` on it before exiting

That's the whole program — no address, no `bind()`, no network activity yet.

- You'll need `<unistd.h>` for `close()`, in addition to `<sys/socket.h>`
